reason_text: A production-exposed HTTP endpoint accepts a filename derived from the request path, treats part of that filename as the user id for an ownership check, and then concatenates the untrusted filename to an attacker-specific per-user download directory and opens it with FileInputStream — without canonicalizing or validating that the final path stays inside the intended base directory. An authenticated attacker (normal user) can craft a filename containing path-traversal elements (e.g. "../../secretfile_export_<their-id>.zip") that will pass the ownership check (the check only parses the id substring) and cause the code to open an arbitrary filesystem path outside the intended download directory. This meets the CWE-22 conditions (attacker-controlled input → file sink → escape via ../ and no safe containment).

  * File: [/repo/dspace-api/src/main/java/org/dspace/app/itemexport/ItemExportServiceImpl.java:838-846]

- Ownership check is insufficient (parses id from filename but does not verify the filename contains no traversal): [repo/dspace-api/src/main/java/org/dspace/app/itemexport/ItemExportServiceImpl.java:916-937]
  * File: [/repo/dspace-api/src/main/java/org/dspace/app/itemexport/ItemExportServiceImpl.java:916-937]
    - lines 923-930: the method extracts the substring between last '_' and last '.' and compares it to eperson.getID().toString(), returning true if equal. This allows filenames containing directory traversal ("../") so long as the id substring is present.
WHY THIS IS EXPLOITABLE:
- Entry point is an HTTP servlet exposed to authenticated users (a realistic attacker = remote low-privilege user). The servlet uses request path info to derive the filename, so the filename is attacker-controlled.
- The code opens a FileInputStream on a path built by simple string concatenation of baseDir + separator + fileName with no canonicalization (no getCanonicalPath(), no normalization nor startsWith(base) check), so path traversal elements like ".." will cause the resulting path to resolve outside the intended base directory.

- There is no symlink-aware containment handling, canonicalization, or whitelisting of filenames; thus all four failure conditions in the test are met.

Also reject path separators and ".." sequences from the filename input before concatenation.

reason_text: The JSP UI renders item metadata (the item title) into the page header without escaping, and item metadata can be supplied by remote submitters via the standard submission flow. This yields a stored XSS (CWE-79) in production-exposed pages (e.g. /handle/<id>). The repository shows (1) user input is persisted from request parameters into item metadata, (2) that metadata is read and used without escaping for the page title, and (3) the header JSP writes that title directly into the HTML <title> (and extra head data) without encoding — allowing an attacker to close the title element and inject script that executes in other users’ browsers.
evidence_text:
- Attacker-controlled input (submission writes request parameters into item metadata): [repo/dspace-api/src/main/java/org/dspace/submit/step/DescribeStep.java:232-249] and [repo/dspace-api/src/main/java/org/dspace/submit/step/DescribeStep.java:272-277]. These lines show request parameters are read and passed directly to itemService.addMetadata(..., vals[z]) / itemService.addMetadata(..., thisVal) without escaping, i.e. user-supplied form values are persisted.

- Unescaped reading of stored metadata into a title string used for page rendering: [repo/dspace-jspui/src/main/webapp/display-item.jsp:90-101] (the code loads the item's dc.title into the "title" variable) and [repo/dspace-jspui/src/main/webapp/display-item.jsp:125] (the subsequent dspace:layout tag is invoked with title="<%= title %>").

- Layout tag stores the passed title into the request attribute without performing escaping: [repo/dspace-jspui/src/main/java/org/dspace/app/webui/jsptag/LayoutTag.java:256-260] (request.setAttribute("dspace.layout.title", title)).

- Page header renders the layout title directly into HTML <title> with no escaping: [repo/dspace-jspui/src/main/webapp/layout/header-default.jsp:47-49] ("<title><%= siteName %>: <%= title %></title>"). Because the title is unescaped, a malicious title like "</title><script>/*...*/</script>" would break out of the title element and execute script in the victim's browser when the page is viewed.

- The repository contains an HTML-escaping helper that is used elsewhere, demonstrating that encoding is available but simply not used in this path: [repo/dspace-api/src/main/java/org/dspace/core/Utils.java:267-281] (addEntities calls Escape.html(...)), and e.g. metadata rendering in ItemTag uses this escaping function: [repo/dspace-jspui/src/main/java/org/dspace/app/webui/jsptag/ItemTag.java:640-643] and [repo/dspace-jspui/src/main/java/org/dspace/app/webui/jsptag/ItemTag.java:674-676] (Utils.addEntities applied when printing metadata in other contexts).

Conclusion: The code path demonstrates all four required conditions: (1) attacker-controlled input (submission form parameters persisted in metadata), (2) the data flows to a web page (display-item.jsp via dspace:layout) that is served in production via HandleServlet, (3) the metadata is output into an HTML context (the <title>) without escaping so it can break out and execute script, and (4) no framework escaping is applied on that path. Therefore the test fails (CWE-79 present).

If you want, I can draft a minimal remediation (escape the title before passing to layout, e.g., Utils.addEntities(title) or ensure LayoutTag/header-default.jsp escape request attributes before printing).

reason_text: The server accepts dataId/group/tenant from a production HTTP API (ConfigController) and uses them directly to build File paths which are written/read/deleted without canonicalization or symlink-safe containment checks. The parameter validation (ParamUtils.isValid) allows dot characters, so an attacker-controlled segment of ".." can be supplied and will cause the resulting File (parent, "..") to resolve outside the intended directory. There is no post-construction realpath/canonicalization-and-compare containment check.
evidence_text:
- Entry point (production HTTP API accepts attacker-controlled file identifiers): ConfigController publish endpoint accepts dataId/group/tenant from remote requests. [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigController.java:119-126] and it checks parameters via ParamUtils before persisting: [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigController.java:143-146]. The controller is mounted at Constants.CONFIG_CONTROLLER_PATH = "/v1/cs/configs" (public API): [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/constant/Constants.java:112-121].

- Parameter validation is insufficient to prevent traversal: ParamUtils.isValid allows '.' characters (and thus the string ".."), and checkParam uses isValid to accept dataId/group (no prohibition of "." sequences): [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/ParamUtils.java:31-36, 53-65, 76-86, 159-166]. Specifically isValid() allows '.' (validChars contains '.') so a value of ".." passes validation.

- Dataflow to a filesystem sink: ConfigCacheService.dump calls DiskUtil.saveToDisk(...) which writes content to a File computed from the dataId/group/tenant: [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/service/ConfigCacheService.java:106-116] (DiskUtil.saveToDisk invocation at line 114). DiskUtil.saveToDisk constructs the target File and writes it: [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/DiskUtil.java:50-60, 107-117]. There is no canonicalization or containment check before writing.

- Example of the escape (why ".." matters): DiskUtil.targetFile builds File objects by successive new File(parent, child) calls and returns the File directly (no normalization): [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/utils/DiskUtil.java:107-117]. Passing a child string of ".." produces a path that, once resolved by the OS (parent + File.separator + ".."), points outside the intended subdirectory. Because there is no getCanonicalPath()/toRealPath() check or startsWith(base) check, the code will write/read/delete that resolved path.

- Additional related sink: Zip extraction writes entries to disk using entry.getName() without path sanitization (Zip Slip): DiskUtils.decompress uses entry.getName() and writes to new File(Paths.get(outputDir, fileName).toString()) and then writes the file contents, without validating that the resulting File is within outputDir: [repo/sys/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/sys/utils/DiskUtils.java:421-431, 432-437]. An attacker who can upload a zip (ConfigController.importAndPublishConfig accepts MultipartFile uploads at the same public API: [repo/config/src/main/java/com/alibaba/nacos/config/server/controller/ConfigController.java:552-558] and unzips it with ZipUtils.unzip) could craft entries with ../ segments in their names — and DiskUtils.decompress would later write such entries to arbitrary filesystem locations (no containment check).

Summary: All four required conditions (production-reachable HTTP entry points accepting attacker-controlled names; those values reaching filesystem write/read/delete sinks; ability to escape the intended directory via "." segments (e.g. "..") since validation permits dot; and absence of canonicalization/containment checks) are present in the repository — therefore this test FAILs (exploitable CWE-22 path traversal / Zip Slip-style issues).

Notes / Recommendations (not required by verdict): validate and strictly whitelist allowed characters (disallow "." alone or sequences like ".."), canonicalize paths (File.getCanonicalPath or Path#toRealPath) and verify the result is a child of the intended base directory, and sanitize zip entry names before extracting (reject absolute names or names containing ".."/separators).

evidence_text:

- Runtime attachment of a BlobDownloader to received blob messages (so downloads happen on the client when messages are processed):
  - [repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/ActiveMQMessageConsumer.java:628-635] (createActiveMQMessage): when a message with type ACTIVEMQ_BLOB_MESSAGE is created on receive, the client calls ((ActiveMQBlobMessage)m).setBlobDownloader(new BlobDownloader(session.getBlobTransferPolicy())); This shows that the client attaches a BlobDownloader (which performs local download operations) to incoming messages at runtime.

- Dataflow to a filesystem sink with no containment checks: FileSystemBlobStrategy.getFile() constructs a java.io.File directly from the message URL and FileInputStream/FileOutputStream are used to read/write that File. There is no canonicalization or base-directory check applied to the message-supplied path.
  - [repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/blob/FileSystemBlobStrategy.java:115-132] (getFile):
    - If message.getURL() != null, it does: return new File(message.getURL().toURI()); (no restriction/normalization/allowlist)
  - [repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/blob/FileSystemBlobStrategy.java:69-78, 83-92] show the implementations that open FileOutputStream/FileInputStream on the File returned by getFile(): uploadStream uses new FileOutputStream(f) and getInputStream returns new FileInputStream(getFile(message)). These are OS filesystem sinks.

- Policy selection and runtime reachability: BlobTransferPolicy.createDownloadStrategy() (and createUploadStrategy()) selects FileSystemBlobStrategy when the configured upload/download URL uses the file: protocol (i.e., file://...). The broker can advertise an upload URL (BrokerInfo.brokerUploadUrl) and the client will pick up that brokerUploadUrl. Thus, if a client is configured (explicitly or via brokerAdvertised info) to use a file:// upload URL the FileSystemBlobStrategy will be used for downloads. See:
  - [repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/blob/BlobTransferPolicy.java:124-173] where createDownloadStrategy checks url.getProtocol().equalsIgnoreCase("FILE") and selects FileSystemBlobStrategy.
  - [repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/ActiveMQConnection.java:1871] (usage): connection handles broker info and sets the client's BlobTransferPolicy brokerUploadUrl from BrokerInfo (so server-advertised brokerUploadUrl influences client strategy selection).

Why this meets the 4-part test for FAIL:
1) Entry point: ActiveMQ producers (remote clients) can set the ActiveMQBlobMessage remote URL (remoteBlobUrl / URL) when sending messages. That is a production-exposed interface (JMS producers). Evidence: ActiveMQBlobMessage.getRemoteBlobUrl()/setRemoteBlobUrl are public fields used to convey the URL across the wire ([repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/command/ActiveMQBlobMessage.java:55-77]).
2) Dataflow: The message URL is used by FileSystemBlobStrategy.getFile() -> new File(message.getURL().toURI()) and then opened via FileInputStream/FileOutputStream in the download/upload code paths ([repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/blob/FileSystemBlobStrategy.java:115-132] and [repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/blob/FileSystemBlobStrategy.java:75-83]). The consumer attaches a BlobDownloader to incoming blob messages at receive time, making this runtime-reachable on the client side ([repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/ActiveMQMessageConsumer.java:628-635]).
3) Escape: The URL is converted to a File directly (via URL.toURI()), so a message URL like file:///etc/passwd or file:///../../somewhere will map to absolute filesystem paths or otherwise escape any intended base; no normalization or canonical-base checks are present in getFile() before opening the File. The code path accepts arbitrary file: URLs and constructs Files from them.
4) No effective containment: There is no check that the constructed File is under an intended base directory (no getCanonicalPath startsWith(base) or similar). The code does not canonicalize+verify nor enforce an allowlist of filenames. FileSystemBlobStrategy.createRootFolder() creates a rootFile used for uploads, but the download path branch bypasses that and directly constructs the File from the message URL without containment checks ([repo/activemq-client/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/blob/FileSystemBlobStrategy.java:115-132]).

Notes / scope clarifications:
- This is a client-side issue: the vulnerable sink occurs in the client blob download/upload strategy (activemq-client module). It is reachable in real deployments when a client is configured to use the file: (FILE) protocol for its BlobTransferPolicy (either explicitly via client config or via broker-advertised brokerUploadUrl). When that configuration is in place, receiving a malicious ActiveMQBlobMessage from an attacker-controlled producer can cause the client to open arbitrary local filesystem paths.
- Whether this is exploitable in a specific deployment depends on whether clients use the FileSystemBlobStrategy for downloads (i.e., have a file:// upload URL configured). The code makes it possible and does not defensively validate the message-supplied path.

1) Unescaped insertion into JavaScript in the web UI (server-side template): message.jsp inserts JMSDestination and JMSMessageID directly into JS code without using <c:out> or other escaping. [activemq-web-console/src/main/webapp/message.jsp:228-241]

     228	function confirmAction(id, action) {

     237		url += "&JMSDestination=${requestContext.messageQuery.JMSDestination}";
     238		url += "&messageId=${row.JMSMessageID}&JMSDestinationType=queue&secret=${sessionScope['secret']}";
     239		if (confirm("Are you sure?"))

   - Because these EL expressions are not wrapped with <c:out> or otherwise escaped, the raw destination/message-id text is emitted into script source. Inserting untrusted characters here can break out of the intended context and inject executable JS.

3) MessageQuery / QueueBrowseQuery use the JMSDestination (request param) to create a QueueBrowser and fetch messages for that destination, demonstrating the dataflow from the request-supplied destination through to the page that renders the message view. [activemq-web/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/web/MessageQuery.java:57-66] and [activemq-web/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/web/QueueBrowseQuery.java:1-60]

4) The web console is a production-exposed web application (servlet mappings) and by default the broker listens on public transport connectors (i.e. remote clients can connect and produce messages / create destinations):
   - web.xml exposes the web console and maps the Spring DispatcherServlet and *.action routes: [activemq-web-console/src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml:94-103]
   - activemq example config shows transport connectors listening on 0.0.0.0 (network-exposed): [activemq-all/src/main/resources/activemq.xml:98-104]

[activemq-web-console/src/main/webapp/queues.jsp:72-85]

reason_text: The codebase contains a runtime-reachable path where attacker-controlled names (e.g. ZIP entry names or other message headers derived from untrusted HTTP request bodies) can flow into the file producer and be used directly to build filesystem paths without canonical containment checks that survive resolution. Specifically: an HTTP consumer reads request bodies into Exchanges; ZipFileDataFormat.unmarshal places the ZIP entry name into Exchange.FILE_NAME; GenericFileProducer.createFileName concatenates endpoint base directory + the header value and only normalizes path separators (it does not remove or resolve ".." path segments); FileOperations.storeFile then constructs a java.io.File from that name and writes to disk. This combination allows an attacker who can send an HTTP request containing a ZIP with a crafted entry name (e.g. "../../outside.txt") to cause the framework to write outside the intended base directory (CWE-22), because no canonicalize-and-verify containment check exists.
evidence_text:
- HTTP request bodies are mapped into Exchanges by the HTTP binding (production-exposed consumer). See DefaultHttpBinding.readRequest which reads the request body into the message and populates HTTP headers, proving an HTTP client can supply content used by later processors: [repo/components/camel-http-common/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/http/common/DefaultHttpBinding.java:102-111] and request headers/path are put into the exchange: [repo/components/camel-http-common/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/http/common/DefaultHttpBinding.java:120-131]. An example Jetty consumer (production HTTP endpoint) in tests demonstrates a route that receives HTTP requests: from("jetty:http://localhost:{{port}}/test") — see a concrete test route that receives HTTP requests and forwards to a route: [repo/components/camel-jetty9/src/test/java/org/apache/camel/component/jetty/ConvertPayloadToInputStreamTest.java:33-41] and route builder lines creating the jetty consumer: [repo/components/camel-jetty9/src/test/java/org/apache/camel/component/jetty/ConvertPayloadToInputStreamTest.java:58-63].

- Untrusted archive entry → Exchange.FILE_NAME: ZipFileDataFormat.unmarshal sets the exchange FILE_NAME header directly from the zip entry name (no sanitization): [repo/components/camel-zipfile/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/dataformat/zipfile/ZipFileDataFormat.java:91-99] (entry.getName() -> exchange.getOut().setHeader(FILE_NAME, entry.getName())).

- FILE_NAME header is used directly to build target filesystem path: GenericFileProducer.createFileName reads Exchange.FILE_NAME (or expression), concatenates the endpoint base directory and the provided name (baseDir + name), and only calls FileUtil.normalizePath which only replaces path separators (it does NOT resolve/remove ".." segments): [repo/camel-core/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/file/GenericFileProducer.java:353-376] and normalization: [repo/camel-core/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/file/GenericFileProducer.java:381-384].

- normalizePath only swaps slash characters and does not neutralize "..": FileUtil.normalizePath only converts path separators and does not remove ".." segments (so "base/../outside" remains): [repo/camel-core/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/util/FileUtil.java:67-79].

- The file is created and written without canonical containment checks: FileOperations.storeFile constructs a java.io.File from the computed name and writes the data (no getCanonicalPath() and no startsWith(baseDir) containment verification): [repo/camel-core/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/file/FileOperations.java:215-223] and the subsequent writing logic (stream/write) performs the write using that File: [repo/camel-core/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/file/FileOperations.java:300-336].

- Inconsistent handling: createTempFileName does compact (collapse) ".." segments via FileUtil.compactPath, but createFileName does not — showing the path is not normalized in a symlink/canonical-safe way for the normal write path: [repo/camel-core/src/main/java/org/apache/camel/component/file/GenericFileProducer.java:415-422] (compactPath used only for temp names).

ASSESSMENT OF CONDITIONS (per rubric):
1) Entry point: HTTP consumer (Jetty/Servlet/other HTTP components) reads request bodies into Exchanges (production-exposed endpoints). The repository includes the HTTP binding and Jetty consumer that map HTTP request bodies to exchanges (see cited files). An attacker can supply a ZIP archive via HTTP request body.
2) Dataflow: The ZIP entry name is placed into Exchange.FILE_NAME by ZipFileDataFormat.unmarshal; GenericFileProducer reads Exchange.FILE_NAME to build the target filename; FileOperations.storeFile writes the file to disk — the code path is clearly present in the repository.
3) Escape: The producer concatenates baseDir + name and only performs simple separator normalization; it does not resolve/canonicalize and check containment. Thus a crafted name with ".." or absolute/other path tricks will result in a java.io.File pointing outside the intended directory when resolved by the OS. No canonical containment check prevents this.
4) No effective containment: There is no evidence of a canonicalize-then-verify check (e.g., getCanonicalPath and comparison to baseDir) anywhere in the file write code. The write path lacks a robust allowlist/containment check.

Conclusion: the repository contains code where an attacker-supplied archive entry name (via an HTTP body to a consumer route that unmarshals zip and writes to file:) can be used to escape the intended directory and write files elsewhere — this meets the CWE-22 conditions.

RECOMMENDATION (brief): When building a target File from an external name, the producer should resolve the final target's canonical path and verify it is within the intended base directory (e.g., target.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(baseDir.getCanonicalPath())), and/or strip/deny path traversal constructs from incoming names (e.g. remove leading separators, collapse ".." entries safely, and/or only allow a filename whitelist).

However, the repo also contains filtering logic that blocks headers that start with "Camel" (which protects many other scripting endpoints such as Velocity/MVEL/JSR223 that use "Camel*" header names). Whether this is an actual CWE-94 (executable code injection) depends on two deployment/runtime facts that cannot be determined from static code alone:

Mustache is generally a logic-less templating engine, but behavior depends on the runtime Mustache implementation and the concrete data model (e.g., whether property access can reach sensitive methods or lambdas are supported). The source code shows the Mustache template is executed with a variable map exposing Exchange and CamelContext objects, which could increase risk if Mustache allows calling methods on those objects.

Whether such a route is present and reachable in production depends on how Camel is used (route definitions) and whether operators intentionally expose Mustache endpoints to untrusted clients.

The worker executes the prepareProject() at runtime when running that task, so this is runtime-reachable in production.

reason_text: I inspected the codebase for runtime filesystem sinks that use attacker-controlled path components reachable from production-exposed interfaces and found no evidence that untrusted remote/low-privilege input can reach an OS filesystem operation in a way that would allow escaping a restricted directory. Filesystem sinks that do construct paths from inputs (1) are built from framework/service configuration or local service instance metadata (operator or service-controlled), not from unauthenticated remote requests, and (2) are used by local-only features (e.g., QoS limited to localhost by default). Therefore there is no provable, production-reachable CWE-22 path in this repository.
evidence_text:
- File sink and path build: FileSystemDynamicConfiguration constructs file paths from group/key and performs file I/O (write/delete/read/watch) using those paths. It creates File objects with the joined path: [repo/dubbo-common/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/common/config/configcenter/file/FileSystemDynamicConfiguration.java:213-219] and [repo/dubbo-common/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/common/config/configcenter/file/FileSystemDynamicConfiguration.java:346-366]. These are filesystem sinks that would be relevant to CWE-22 if fed by untrusted input.
  - Specifically: configFile(String key, String group) -> new File(buildPathKey(group, key)) [repo/dubbo-common/.../FileSystemDynamicConfiguration.java:213-215]
  - doPublishConfig/doRemoveConfig/doGetConfig call write/delete/read on those File objects [repo/dubbo-common/.../FileSystemDynamicConfiguration.java:347-358, 361-366].

- Path normalization behavior (important for traversal analysis): TreePathDynamicConfiguration builds pathKey with PathUtils.buildPath -> PathUtils.normalize. PathUtils.normalize removes query strings and duplicate slashes but does NOT resolve or remove ".." components nor canonicalize paths, so it would not by itself prevent traversal if the inputs were attacker-controlled: [repo/dubbo-common/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/common/config/configcenter/TreePathDynamicConfiguration.java:130-136] and [repo/dubbo-common/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/common/utils/PathUtils.java:36-45, 57-72].

- Who supplies the key/group used for those paths (source / trust analysis): the usages of DynamicConfiguration.publishConfig/configFile in the codebase are called from library/service code that uses service instance IDs / service names or operator-provided configuration values (not remote user HTTP/RPC inputs):
  - FileSystemServiceDiscovery.doRegister calls dynamicConfiguration.publishConfig(serviceInstanceId, serviceName, content) where serviceInstanceId comes from the local ServiceInstance object (ServiceInstance.getId() or host+port) and serviceName from the ServiceInstance — these represent local service metadata, i.e. service process-controlled/administrator-controlled values, not remote request parameters: [repo/dubbo-registry/dubbo-registry-api/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/registry/client/FileSystemServiceDiscovery.java:136-143] and getServiceInstanceId() definition [repo/dubbo-registry/.../FileSystemServiceDiscovery.java:110-116].
  - AbstractRegistry / AbstractMetadataReport use filename parameters that come from the configured registry/metadata-report URLs (URL parameters such as dubbo.registry.file or dubbo.metadata.file). Those are operator configuration values passed at startup, not directly from remote users: [repo/dubbo-registry/dubbo-registry-api/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/registry/support/AbstractRegistry.java:99-106] and [repo/dubbo-metadata/dubbo-metadata-api/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/metadata/report/support/AbstractMetadataReport.java:103-111].

- Production-exposed interfaces check (QoS / HTTP handlers): code that accepts remote connections (HTTP handlers, QoS telnet/HTTP) either do not perform arbitrary filesystem writes with request-supplied filenames or are bound to localhost by default:
  - HTTP RPC handlers (e.g., HttpProtocol.InternalHandler) pass request bodies to JsonRpcServer to invoke service methods; they do not construct filesystem paths from HTTP parameters: [repo/dubbo-rpc/dubbo-rpc-http/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/rpc/protocol/http/HttpProtocol.java:78-96].
  - QoS command decoding and execution (HTTP/Telnet) are present, but the allowlist for remote QoS access blocks foreign IPs by default (LocalHostPermitHandler rejects non-loopback unless configured otherwise), so QoS commands are not remotely accessible absent explicit operator configuration: [repo/dubbo-plugin/dubbo-qos/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/qos/server/handler/LocalHostPermitHandler.java:31-46]. The QoS commands implemented in the repository that operate on files (e.g., LogTelnetHandler reads the configured log file) use configured logger file(s) and do not accept arbitrary filenames from remote users: [repo/dubbo-plugin/dubbo-qos/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/qos/legacy/LogTelnetHandler.java:46-59, 57-72].

Conclusion rationale: The only code that constructs filesystem paths from values that could contain path separators (group/key, filenames) is fed from internal/administrator/service-controlled sources (URL config parameters, service instance metadata). I did not find any production-exposed endpoint (HTTP/RPC/WebSocket, uploaded filenames, untrusted DB fields the attacker can write, or pub/sub messages the attacker can publish) that allows a low-privilege or remote attacker to supply those file path components at runtime. Therefore the four conditions required to mark this test FAIL (production-reachable attacker-controlled source → dataflow to filesystem sink → ability to escape intended base → lack of containment) are not all satisfied by evidence in the repository.

If you want deeper verification, possible next steps (not required to reach this verdict but useful if you want to be extra cautious):
- Confirm how the product is deployed in your environment and whether any of the configuration URL parameters (e.g., dubbo.registry.file, dubbo.metadata.file, or dynamic-configuration group/key) might be writable by an untrusted remote user in your production setup. If such an operator-exposed configuration can be changed by attackers at runtime (for example, via a management HTTP API), re-evaluate the code paths above with that deployment detail.
- If you want me to try to construct a concrete exploit proof-of-concept, I would need runtime access or a live deployment to confirm reachable endpoints and show a path traversal that escapes a configured base directory; without execution I can only reason from code.

Given the repository code and its documented/observable usage, I assess this test as PASS.

reason_text: I examined the repository for any production-reachable flows where attacker-controlled input (HTTP requests) is written into HTML/JS/DOM-executable contexts that would be served to other users without correct context-aware escaping. The project provides HTTP/REST/JSON-RPC/SOAP handlers, but they delegate to JSON-RPC, RESTEasy, or SOAP handlers that operate on request/response streams and produce JSON/XML/soap payloads rather than HTML pages or script-bearing HTML. I found no code that renders user-supplied values into HTML/JavaScript contexts (no text/html responses, no template rendering into HTML, and no dangerous DOM APIs or inline script generation in the repo). Therefore there is no evidence of an exploitable CWE-79 vulnerability in this codebase.
evidence_text:

This uses RESTEasy to handle and produce REST responses (typically JSON/XML), not server-side HTML templates.

- No occurrences of HTML-serving code patterns were found in the repository search. I saved the grep outputs (empty files show no matches) as artifacts: /evidence/artifacts/grep_text_html.txt (no "text/html" occurrences) and /evidence/artifacts/grep_html_like.txt (no occurrences of <script, <html, innerHTML, document.write, onclick=, onload=, javascript:). You can inspect them here: [/evidence/artifacts/grep_text_html.txt] and [/evidence/artifacts/grep_html_like.txt].
- The only code that mentions HTML escaping is in a code generator used to escape comments for generated JavaDoc (compile-time artifact), not runtime HTML served to end users: [repo/compiler/src/main/java/org/apache/dubbo/gen/AbstractGenerator.java:176-194] (HtmlEscapers.htmlEscaper used for JavaDoc generation).

Notes / Threat model clarification: The repository exposes HTTP endpoints that are reachable by remote clients (DispatcherServlet + HttpBinder usage). However, the handlers in this repository produce JSON-RPC/REST/SOAP responses or forward streams to framework handlers rather than rendering HTML pages or injecting unescaped input into HTML/JS contexts. Under the provided attacker/victim model this means there is no demonstrated path where attacker-controlled input from a remote user is placed into an HTML/JS/DOM-executable sink that other users' browsers would execute.

Conclusion: Based on static inspection of the codebase and the absence of HTML output sinks or unsafe client-side DOM APIs, the test that "There is no exploitable CWE-79" PASSES for this repository.

evidence_text:

Why this is INCONCLUSIVE:
- The codebase contains both a risky encoder (that preserves '/') and multiple sanitization steps (split/truncate on upload, MarkupParser.cleanLink on parent page when resolving an attachment name) so the actual runtime path sent to the filesystem provider often appears to have slashes removed before BasicAttachmentProvider builds the file path.
- To demonstrate an exploitable CWE-22 we must show a reachable HTTP request (exact URL pattern and parameters) that results in an unsanitized path containing ".." or "/" elements reaching a filesystem sink (e.g., FileInputStream/FileOutputStream) under BasicAttachmentProvider (or other provider), and the code performing file operations without canonicalization or startsWith(base) checks. I could not find a single code path that unambiguously preserves attacker-controlled slashes/.. into a File constructor and then uses that File without canonicalization.

What additional information / tests are needed to conclude PASS or FAIL:
1) Concrete runtime endpoint and example HTTP request that you expect to be attackable. Provide the URL path used for attachments in your deployed web.xml / servlet mapping (the servlet mapping for the attachment servlet; e.g., is AttachmentServlet mapped to something like /wiki/attach/*?).
2) A reproducible runtime test: start the webapp and make an HTTP GET/PUT/POST to the attachment endpoint with a path containing traversal elements (for example: a request whose pathInfo is "/../../somewhere/TargetPage/evil.txt" or similar). Observe the server logs and filesystem to see whether files are read/written outside the intended m_storageDir or page directory.
3) Alternatively, confirm that upstream normalization always removes slashes before provider methods are invoked (for example, a statement of policy and mapping showing that parsePageFromURL outputs are always run through MarkupParser.cleanLink before provider APIs are called in the ATTACH flow). reason_text: The SFTP subsystem accepts attacker-controlled remote paths (SFTP commands) and resolves them into OS filesystem operations under a "rooted" (sandbox) file system, but the provider checks containment using normalize()/startsWith(root) without performing OS-level canonicalization (toRealPath) on the resolved path. That allows symlink-based escapes: a path that refers to a symlink inside the sandbox which points outside will pass the startsWith(root) check yet will be dereferenced by the underlying filesystem operations, enabling access outside the intended root.
evidence_text:
- Entry point (remote attacker-controlled SFTP path parameter): AbstractSftpSubsystemHelper reads client-supplied path strings from the SFTP request buffer and passes them to resolveFile (→ used by open/create/etc.). See where the path is read and forwarded to doOpen:
  - [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/AbstractSftpSubsystemHelper.java:432-436] (reads path from buffer)
  - [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/SftpSubsystem.java:859-867] (doOpen calls resolveFile and then opens the resulting Path)

- Dataflow to OS filesystem sinks (open/read/write): FileHandle ultimately calls SftpFileSystemAccessor.openFile which by default opens a FileChannel on the Path, delegating to the platform filesystem:
  - [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/FileHandle.java:70-76] (calls accessor.openFile(...))
  - [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/SftpFileSystemAccessor.java:84-89] (default openFile uses FileChannel.open(file,...))

- Where virtual/sandboxed FS is created (production usage): VirtualFileSystemFactory constructs a RootedFileSystem via RootedFileSystemProvider (this is the documented/supported sandbox mechanism):
  - [repo/sshd-core/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/common/file/virtualfs/VirtualFileSystemFactory.java:68-76] (createFileSystem returns new RootedFileSystemProvider().newFileSystem(dir,...))
  - README references the VirtualFileSystemFactory / RootedFileSystem as the sandbox: [repo/README.md:417-421]

- Containment check uses normalize() but does NOT use OS canonicalization (toRealPath) on the resolved path before comparing with the canonicalized root. Root is canonicalized when the filesystem is created, but resolved user paths are only normalized and checked with startsWith(root):
  - Root canonicalization when filesystem is created: newFileSystem(...) uses ensureDirectory(path).toRealPath(); root stored as real path: [repo/sshd-core/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/common/file/root/RootedFileSystemProvider.java:93-95]
  - Path resolution for requests: resolveLocalPath builds resolved = root.resolve(subPath); resolved = resolved.normalize(); resolved = resolved.toAbsolutePath(); then checks startsWith(root) (NO toRealPath on resolved): [repo/sshd-core/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/common/file/root/RootedFileSystemProvider.java:481-501]
    - Lines: 487-490 show normalize() and toAbsolutePath(); 499-501 show the startsWith(root) check and rejection only if check fails.

- Following symlinks / lack of symlink-safe containment: the code uses normalized paths and then delegates to the underlying provider to actually open/read files. The underlying file operations (FileChannel.open, Files.*) will follow symlinks on the OS when performing I/O, meaning a path that points to a symlink inside the root that resolves (at OS-level) to a location outside the root will be accessed successfully despite the startsWith(root) check. Evidence that underlying provider is used for actual I/O:
  - RootedFileSystemProvider.newByteChannel / newInputStream etc. call unroot(path) then delegate to the native provider: [repo/sshd-core/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/common/file/root/RootedFileSystemProvider.java:156-167, 170-175, 186-191]
  - unroot(...) -> resolveLocalPath(...) performs normalize-based check (no realpath) as shown above: [repo/sshd-core/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/common/file/root/RootedFileSystemProvider.java:450-458 and 481-501]

- SFTP supports symbolic-link operations (clients can create and reference symlinks) and the subsystem follows links by default (AUTO_FOLLOW_LINKS default true). See definitions and handling:
  - AUTO_FOLLOW_LINKS default: [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/AbstractSftpSubsystemHelper.java:115-121]
  - SFTP symlink commands and createLink handling: [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/AbstractSftpSubsystemHelper.java:733-752] and concrete createLink implementation in SftpSubsystem that calls Files.createSymbolicLink(link, existing): [repo/sshd-sftp/src/main/java/org/apache/sshd/server/subsystem/sftp/SftpSubsystem.java:342-356]

Summary of the issue: The code enforces containment by comparing a normalized absolute Path string to the canonical root, but does not canonicalize the resolved path with the OS (no toRealPath/canonicalization) before the startsWith check. That leaves a class of escapes via filesystem symlinks: if an attacker-controlled path references a symlink located inside the sandbox whose target resides outside the sandbox, the normalized path check will succeed (it still starts with the sandbox root), and the subsequent OS-level file operations will follow the symlink and access files outside the sandbox. Therefore the repository contains a CWE-22 style path-escape vulnerability reachable from production-exposed SFTP commands.

Notes / caveats:
- Exploitability requires a symlink (or other filesystem alias) inside the sandbox that points outside the sandbox. Whether an attacker can create that symlink via SFTP depends on the server configuration and which operations are permitted; SFTP includes symlink creation support (SSH_FXP_SYMLINK), but creation of a symlink whose target would be rejected by resolveLocalPath may be blocked. Nevertheless, the core check is insufficiently robust because it does not canonicalize the resolved path to account for symlinks: the intended containment test should canonicalize (toRealPath) the resolved path (or otherwise ensure symlink-safe containment) before comparing with the canonical root.

Recommendation (brief): perform a realpath/canonicalization (e.g., Path.toRealPath(LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS) or appropriate OS-level canonical resolution while avoiding race conditions) on the resolved path before comparing with the canonical root, or implement symlink-safe checks (and/or open with NOFOLLOW and additional checks) to ensure true containment.

All cited file/line evidence above exists in the repository at the paths shown and can be independently inspected.

reason_text: The repository contains at least one production-reachable code path where externally-controlled data (registry event fields derived from user-supplied metadata) is appended, without neutralization, to an OS command invocation and is executed. The dataflow: remote user -> Registry event field (e.g. flow version comments) -> ScriptEventHookProvider builds ProcessBuilder command list using event.getFields() values -> builder.start() executes the script with those event field values as arguments. Because the event field values are passed directly as process arguments (no sanitization or allowlist), an attacker who can provide event content (e.g. version comments) can influence the executed command's arguments and thereby change the intended behavior of the invoked script.
evidence_text:
- The ScriptEventHookProvider adds event fields as command arguments and starts the process: [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-framework/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/provider/hook/ScriptEventHookProvider.java:1-120] specifically:
  - command construction: command.add(arg.getValue()); (shows event field values are appended as-is)
  - execution: final ProcessBuilder builder = new ProcessBuilder(command); ... builder.start();
  See lines around the creation and start of the ProcessBuilder and the loop adding event fields as arguments.

- The EventFactory creates events that include user-supplied content in fields: [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-framework/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/event/EventFactory.java:1-120]
  - In flowVersionCreated(...) the code sets the COMMENT field using snapshot metadata comments:
    final String versionComments = versionedFlowSnapshot.getSnapshotMetadata().getComments() == null ? "" : versionedFlowSnapshot.getSnapshotMetadata().getComments();
    .addField(EventFieldName.COMMENT, versionComments)
  This shows that event fields can contain free-form comments supplied by the user who created the version.

- The Event/EventField interfaces show fields are plain strings accessible via getValue():
  - Event: [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-provider-api/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/hook/Event.java:1-60]
  - EventField: [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-provider-api/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/hook/EventField.java:1-60]
  These interfaces confirm event fields are string values taken from domain objects and are passed to providers like ScriptEventHookProvider.

Why this meets the CWE-78 criteria (mapped to the test's four conditions):
1) Entry point (attacker-controlled source): Event fields include e.g. version comments that come from VersionedFlowSnapshot snapshot metadata (.getComments()) — these are provided by the user creating the flow version (a production-exposed API). See EventFactory.flowVersionCreated adding the COMMENT field with versionComments.
2) Dataflow to sink: ScriptEventHookProvider collects event.getFields(), appends each EventField.getValue() to the command list, constructs a ProcessBuilder with that list, and calls builder.start(). This reaches an OS command execution sink. [ScriptEventHookProvider.java: command.add(arg.getValue()); builder.start();]
3) Command-modification capability: The attacker can control argument strings passed to the executed script. Even though ProcessBuilder is used (argv-style execution), arguments are fed directly to the script and can materially change the script's behavior (e.g., pass flags/options or file paths). This counts as argument/option injection per the test definition.
4) No effective neutralization: There is no sanitization, quotation, or allowlist applied to event field values prior to adding them as arguments. The values are appended unchanged.

Notes and scope clarifications:
- ScriptEventHookProvider is configured by administrators (it requires configuration) but it executes in response to registry events that are triggered by user actions (e.g., creating/updating flows). Under the provided attacker/trust model, the event fields (like comments) are attacker-controlled when they originate from remote users via production-exposed API calls, so this is a valid production attack surface.
- An additional, related pattern to note: there are other ProcessBuilder/Runtime.exec usages in the repo (e.g., ExecuteProcess/ExecuteStreamCommand). Those processors are annotated @Restricted and require EXECUTE_CODE permission (operator-level configuration) so per the instructions they are considered operator/admin-facing and thus treated as trusted/operator-only unless product docs indicate otherwise. The ScriptEventHookProvider path differs because it executes scripts (configured by admin) using event fields that can carry user-supplied values at runtime.

Conclusion: The repo contains a runtime-reachable path where attacker-controlled, production-originating input reaches an OS process invocation as arguments without neutralization, enabling argument injection and therefore failing the CWE-78 check.

reason_text: I reviewed the repository code handling web UI input/output and found the only place where remote input flows into HTML that is actually rendered in a browser is the webconsole Gogo terminal. That dataflow is defended in two ways: (1) the terminal HTML rendering escapes special HTML characters before embedding terminal text into the HTML, preventing injected markup/script from being interpreted by browsers; and (2) access to the webconsole is protected by a JAAS-based WebConsoleSecurityProvider which by default requires authentication and the 'admin' role. Together these mean there is no production-reachable, attacker-controlled input that is rendered into an executable HTML/JS context without proper escaping or sufficient privilege.
evidence_text:

  - Code: "String str = request.getParameter("k");" and later "String dump = st.handle(str, f != null && f.length() > 0);"

  - Code excerpt (escaping):
    - "case '&': sb.append("&"); break;"
    - "case '<': sb.append("<"); break;"
    - "case '>': sb.append(">"); break;"

evidence_text:
1) Client-controlled identifiers in REST API /preserveSourceProperties behavior
   - StandardServiceFacade allows clients to preserve a user-supplied bucket identifier when creating a bucket (preserveSourceProperties=true). [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-web-api/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/web/service/StandardServiceFacade.java:196-205]
     * Lines: [..] if (preserveSourceProperties) { validateIdentifierPresent(bucket, BUCKET_ENTITY_TYPE); } else { validateIdentifierNotPresent(bucket, BUCKET_ENTITY_TYPE); bucket.setIdentifier(UUID.randomUUID().toString()); }
   - StandardServiceFacade allows clients to supply a flow identifier (if provided the server keeps it) when creating a flow (backwards-compatibility). [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-web-api/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/web/service/StandardServiceFacade.java:244-253]
     * Lines: [..] // NOTE: Don't validate that identifier is null... if (versionedFlow.getIdentifier() == null) { versionedFlow.setIdentifier(UUID.randomUUID().toString()); }

2) These identifiers are persisted and used directly as filesystem path components
   - DatabaseMetadataService persists Flow IDs/metadata using the ID value from the FlowEntity without sanitization. [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-framework/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/db/DatabaseMetadataService.java:260-276]
     * Lines: [..] jdbcTemplate.update(itemSql, flow.getId(), ...); jdbcTemplate.update(flowSql, flow.getId());

3) File system sink uses bucket/flow identifiers directly (no neutralization/canonicalization)
   - FileSystemFlowPersistenceProvider constructs directories and writes snapshot files using the (unsanitized) bucket and flow ids and a path built by string concatenation. There is no call to sanitize, no canonicalize/realpath check, and no validation that the resulting path is under the configured flowStorageDir. [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-framework/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/provider/flow/FileSystemFlowPersistenceProvider.java:72-110;181-184]
     * Lines: [..] final File bucketDir = new File(flowStorageDir, context.getBucketId()); ... final File flowDir = new File(bucketDir, context.getFlowId()); ... final File versionFile = new File(versionDir, versionString + SNAPSHOT_EXTENSION); try (final OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream(versionFile)) { ... }
     * getSnapshotFile(): snapshotFilename = bucketId + "/" + flowId + "/" + version + "/" + version + SNAPSHOT_EXTENSION; return new File(flowStorageDir, snapshotFilename);

4) Contrast: bundle persistence sanitizes inputs (showing project is capable of sanitization)
   - FileSystemBundlePersistenceProvider sanitizes bucket/group/artifact inputs via FileUtils.sanitizeFilename before building paths. [repo/nifi-registry/nifi-registry-core/nifi-registry-framework/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/registry/provider/extension/FileSystemBundlePersistenceProvider.java:205-213;233-235]
     * Lines: [..] return new File(bundleStorageDir, sanitize(bucketId) + "/" + sanitize(groupId) + "/" + sanitize(artifactId)); static String sanitize(final String input) { return FileUtils.sanitizeFilename(input).trim().toLowerCase(); }

Why this meets CWE-22 criteria:
- Entry point: The REST API exposes endpoints that let requestors supply bucket and flow identifiers (POST /buckets?preserveSourceProperties=true and POST /buckets/{bucketId}/flows with a body containing an identifier). These endpoints are production-exposed REST endpoints.
- Dataflow: The supplied identifier values are persisted in DB and later flow through RegistryService -> FlowPersistenceProvider into FileSystemFlowPersistenceProvider, which constructs OS filesystem paths that include the identifiers and opens FileOutputStream / InputStream on those paths.
- Escape: Because identifiers are concatenated into path components (and may include path separators and ".." sequences provided by clients) and no normalization/realpath-based containment check is performed, an attacker able to set identifiers can cause the constructed path to resolve outside the configured flowStorageDir.
- No effective containment: There is no canonicalization and allowlist check (e.g., realpath startsWith(flowStorageDir.getCanonicalPath())) in FileSystemFlowPersistenceProvider; nor is there a sanitize step applied to flow IDs/bucket IDs (unlike the bundle provider which sanitizes inputs). Therefore containment is ineffective/absent.

Notes / attacker model: This analysis relies on the fact that identifiers can be supplied by clients via the documented REST API when preserveSourceProperties is used for buckets and flows accept client-supplied identifiers (the code preserves provided flow identifiers). The REST endpoints are production-exposed JAX-RS resources in the repository and authorization checks are performed, but authenticated or authorized clients with the ability to create buckets/flows can exploit this. The project also provides a means (preserveSourceProperties) to persist client-chosen bucket identifiers, so the capability to store arbitrary identifiers is intentionally supported.

Conclusion: The repository contains a code path that satisfies all four requirements for CWE-22 (attacker-controlled path components reach filesystem sink and can escape intended base directory with no effective containment). Therefore the test FAILs.

reason_text: The repo contains a runtime-reachable path where untrusted, production-exposed input (HTTP requests received by ListenHTTP) can influence command execution performed by ExecuteStreamCommand. ExecuteStreamCommand allows its Command Path and arguments to be specified via FlowFile attributes (expression language), evaluates those attributes from incoming FlowFiles, constructs a ProcessBuilder.command(...) from the resulting values, and starts the process. ListenHTTP receives remote HTTP requests and stores request values (e.g., the request URI and selected headers) into FlowFile attributes. An attacker who can send requests to a ListenHTTP endpoint and who is able to cause the flow to route those FlowFiles into an ExecuteStreamCommand processor configured to evaluate those attributes can therefore control which program is executed and/or supply arguments that change the program's behavior. There is no sanitization/neutralization of these attribute values before they are passed into ProcessBuilder.
evidence_text:
- ListenHTTP is a production-exposed HTTP ingress that "Starts an HTTP Server and listens ... to transform incoming requests into FlowFiles": [/workdir/repo/nifi-nar-bundles/nifi-standard-bundle/nifi-standard-processors/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/processors/standard/ListenHTTP.java:84-91]

- ListenHTTP saves request-derived values into FlowFile attributes (these attributes can therefore be attacker-controlled by sending HTTP requests): specifically it puts the request URI and remote host into attributes "restlistener.request.uri" and "restlistener.remote.source.host": [/workdir/repo/nifi-nar-bundles/nifi-standard-bundle/nifi-standard-processors/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/processors/standard/servlets/ListenHTTPServlet.java:447-455]

- ExecuteStreamCommand declares the "Command Path" property to support Expression Language evaluated against FLOWFILE_ATTRIBUTES (i.e., the property value can reference FlowFile attributes): [/workdir/repo/nifi-nar-bundles/nifi-standard-bundle/nifi-standard-processors/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/processors/standard/ExecuteStreamCommand.java:213-219]

- At runtime ExecuteStreamCommand evaluates the configured command property against the incoming FlowFile and adds the resulting value as the first element of the args list (executeCommand -> args[0]): [/workdir/repo/nifi-nar-bundles/nifi-standard-bundle/nifi-standard-processors/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/processors/standard/ExecuteStreamCommand.java:399-401]

- The processor then passes the collected args list directly to ProcessBuilder.command(args) and starts the process with builder.start(): [/workdir/repo/nifi-nar-bundles/nifi-standard-bundle/nifi-standard-processors/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/processors/standard/ExecuteStreamCommand.java:477-493]

- There is no intermediate sanitization or escaping of the attribute-derived values before they are added to the args list and used to start the process (the code uses evaluateAttributeExpressions(...) and then args.add(...) / builder.command(args) directly), demonstrating lack of effective neutralization: [/workdir/repo/nifi-nar-bundles/nifi-standard-bundle/nifi-standard-processors/src/main/java/org/apache/nifi/processors/standard/ExecuteStreamCommand.java:399-401, 438-446, 477-479]

Notes (threat-model evidence):
- ListenHTTP is explicitly an HTTP listener (production-exposed) and populates attributes from the request; ExecuteStreamCommand supports FlowFile attribute expression language. Therefore a deployment that wires ListenHTTP -> ExecuteStreamCommand (a common NiFi flow configuration) would be vulnerable if the operator configures the ExecuteStreamCommand property to reference FlowFile attributes (e.g., ${restlistener.request.uri} or a header attribute). The vulnerability arises at runtime only if the operator configures the processor to use attributes that can be controlled by remote clients; the code paths above show the functionality that enables an attacker to control the executed command.

Conclusion: The repository contains code that enables CWE-78-style command modification via production-reachable HTTP input flowing into ProcessBuilder-based execution, without sanitization. Therefore the test FAILs.

In particular fileName is assigned using substring(ls) (note ls is index of separator), which preserves a leading separator: [repo/hutool-extra/src/main/java/cn/hutool/extra/servlet/multipart/UploadFileHeader.java:168-176].

- Dangerous dataflow to filesystem sink: UploadFile.write(File destination) will, if destination is a directory, construct a new File(destination, header.getFileName()) and then write/move the uploaded bytes (FileUtil.writeBytes or FileUtil.move) to that target without any canonicalization or containment check: [repo/hutool-extra/src/main/java/cn/hutool/extra/servlet/multipart/UploadFile.java:60-100] showing the construction and write/move calls; and the writeBytes / move sinks are real filesystem operations: [repo/hutool-core/src/main/java/cn/hutool/core/io/FileUtil.java:2947-2959] (writeBytes) and [repo/hutool-core/src/main/java/cn/hutool/core/io/FileUtil.java:968-996] (move).

evidence_text:
1) Vulnerable unzip that writes ZIP entries to disk using Utilities.path + startsWith() check (insufficient normalization):
   - [/repo/org.hl7.fhir.r5/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/r5/terminologies/TerminologyCacheManager.java:97-112]
     This method builds the destination path via Utilities.path(targetDir, ze.getName()) and then checks path.startsWith(targetDir) before writing. Because Utilities.path only removes leading ".." components when an argument itself starts with "..", intermediate path segments like "subdir/../evil" are preserved and the startsWith check can be bypassed after normalization, enabling path escape.

2) The path-building logic (Utilities.path) does not fully normalize arbitrary embedded ".." segments inside a single argument:
   - [/repo/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/Utilities.java:617-674]
     Utilities.path handles ".." only at the start of an argument (while (a.startsWith(".." + File.separator)) { ... }) and does not normalize ".." segments that appear later inside the same zip entry name (e.g., "sub/../file"). This makes the startsWith check in (1) insufficient to prevent "zip-slip" style escapes.

3) The vulnerable unzip writes ZIP entry streams to disk via TextFile.streamToFileNoClose:
   - [/repo/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/TextFile.java:244-246]
     TextFile.streamToFileNoClose(stream, filename) writes the entry bytes to the computed filename on disk.

4) Another insecure unzip implementation (Scanner.unzip) builds file paths by simple concatenation without normalization and writes files directly:
   - [/repo/org.hl7.fhir.validation/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/validation/Scanner.java:335-347]
     This code constructs filePath = destDirectory + File.separator + entry.getName() and writes it without validating or canonicalizing the result; it is also susceptible to zip-slip if the ZIP content is attacker-controlled.

5) There is a secure unzip implementation available in the utilities, but it is not used in the vulnerable sites:
   - [/repo/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/Utilities.java:1472-1494] and [/repo/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/utilities/Utilities.java:1501-1516]
     Utilities.unzip(InputStream, Path) uses Path.resolve(...) and normalize() and an explicit startsWith check on the normalized path (zipSlipProtect) to prevent zip-slip correctly. The presence of this safer helper demonstrates an available fix but the vulnerable code paths do not use it.

Why INCONCLUSIVE (detailed):
- The repository contains clear, concrete code that will allow path escapes when extracting ZIP entries to disk if an attacker can control the ZIP entry names (evidence points to CWE-22 style problems in TerminologyCacheManager.unzip and Scanner.unzip). That satisfies steps 2 (dataflow to file sink) and 3 (escape after resolution) of the rubric (I demonstrated problematic path construction and why the check is insufficient). However:
  * Step 1 (Entry point): I could not find unambiguous documentation or code proving that those vulnerable unzip routines are invoked with ZIP data that a remote or low-privilege attacker can supply in production (the code often downloads ZIPs from fixed, trusted hosts like tx.fhir.org or fhir.org, or reads ZIP data from CLI inputs). The threat model requires attacker-controlled input only when the repository/docs show that the input can be supplied by a remote or low-privilege user through a production-exposed interface. That link is not conclusively established in the repo.
  * Step 4 (No effective containment): There is no canonicalization+validation in the vulnerable unzip functions; however whether that matters depends on whether the ZIP input is attacker-controlled in production.

Exactly what additional information is needed to decide PASS vs FAIL:
1) Deployment / runtime usage info: For each vulnerable unzip/write sink (notably TerminologyCacheManager.unzip and Scanner.unzip), please provide answers to:

   - Which parameter or configuration values determine the ZIP source passed to the vulnerable unzip? For TerminologyCacheManager: who supplies ghOrg/ghRepo/ghBranch in production and can any part of them be influenced by an external user? For Scanner.unzip: can destDirectory or the ZIP source be chosen by an external user of a production endpoint?

2) Example runtime calling context or logs showing these methods running on ZIP data from an untrusted source (e.g., server access logs showing a user-supplied URL or uploaded ZIP file that was passed to the unzip function). A small code snippet from the production entry-point showing how user input flows into the unzip call would suffice.

If you can provide the above, I can re-evaluate and produce a PASS if the attacker can indeed control the ZIP content or a FAIL if the inputs are operator-only/trusted.

Short actionable recommendations (safe fixes):
- Replace custom unzip logic with the safe utility that normalizes and checks paths (Utilities.unzip / zipSlipProtect). For example, use Utilities.unzip(zipStream, Path.of(targetDir)) instead of building paths via Utilities.path + startsWith check.

evidence_text:
- The CLI/library entry that evaluates FHIRPath is implemented here; it parses the expression with the project's engine and evaluates to string (no ScriptEngine/Java compiler involved) [repo/org.hl7.fhir.validation/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/validation/ValidationEngine.java:734-740].
- The CLI wrapper that exposes this evaluateFhirpath functionality is a command-line/service API (ValidationService) and calls the library method with cliContext.getFhirpath(); this is a CLI/library usage, not an HTTP endpoint in this repository [repo/org.hl7.fhir.validation/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/validation/cli/services/ValidationService.java:246-249].
- The expression interpreter implementation is the project’s own FHIRPath engine (parser + evaluator) — it is implemented in Java as FHIRPathEngine (an internal interpreter for FHIRPath), not by delegating to a general-purpose dynamic code evaluator like javax.script or a Java compiler at runtime [repo/org.hl7.fhir.r5/src/main/java/org/hl7/fhir/r5/utils/FHIRPathEngine.java:112-119] and throughout that file (the class implements parsing/evaluation of FHIRPath expressions).

However, loading remote resources into the validator leads to parsing/validation by the library’s FHIRPath engine (internal interpreter) rather than executing the loaded data as host-language code. The repository does not itself define any network-exposed endpoint that accepts arbitrary expression text from remote unauthenticated users as part of a production service.

Notes/Clarifications (why not FAIL / not INCONCLUSIVE):
- FAIL would require showing a production-reachable attacker-controlled source that flows into a code-evaluation sink where the attacker can change syntax/behavior and no effective restriction exists. The repo does contain an expression language (FHIRPath) that is parsed and evaluated, and it can load IG content over HTTP; however the only explicit caller of the evaluateFhirPath API in this repo is the CLI/library layer (ValidationService), and the repository contains no server endpoints or docs proving that untrusted remote users in a production deployment can supply expressions that are evaluated by a host-language eval/compile sink. The FHIRPath engine itself is an interpreter for a constrained expression language, implemented inside the project — that means attacker input would be interpreted by the project’s own engine, not by an external host eval, and the test requires evidence of an exploitable evaluation sink (e.g., host-language eval) reachable from an attacker.

reason_text: An HTTP-uploaded filename (MultipartFile.getOriginalFilename) is treated as attacker-controlled (upload endpoint /api/custom/jar), concatenated into an HDFS path without normalization or canonicalization, and then written with fs.create(Path) — allowing an attacker-supplied filename containing path traversal components (e.g. "../") to make the effective path resolve outside the intended per-project/jar-type base directory. There is no canonicalization + startsWith(base) containment check.
evidence_text:
- Entry point (HTTP upload): controller mapping showing the production HTTP endpoint that accepts a file upload and forwards it to the service [repo/src/metadata-server/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/controller/CustomFileController.java:46-56].
  - [/repo/src/metadata-server/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/controller/CustomFileController.java:46-56] shows POST /api/custom/jar receives @RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file and calls customFileService.uploadJar(...).

- Attacker-controllable source (uploaded filename): the service uses MultipartFile.getOriginalFilename() as the jar name with only an extension check (no path sanitization) [repo/src/common-service/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/service/CustomFileService.java:75-82, 104-116, 121-129, 237-246].
  - [/repo/src/common-service/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/service/CustomFileService.java:75-82] uploadJar(...) is invoked by the controller.
  - [/repo/src/common-service/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/service/CustomFileService.java:104-116] checkJarLegal(...) calls checkJarName(jarName) which only ensures the filename ends with ".jar" (no path traversal sanitization).
  - [/repo/src/common-service/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/service/CustomFileService.java:121-129] uploadCustomJar(...) reads jarFile.getOriginalFilename() into jarName and writes the uploaded bytes to an HDFS Path created from the concatenated jar path: "Path path = new Path(jarHdfsPath); try (FSDataOutputStream out = fs.create(path)) { IOUtils.copyBytes(jarFile.getInputStream(), out, 4096, true); }" — this is the filesystem sink.
  - [/repo/src/common-service/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/service/CustomFileService.java:237-239] getJarPath(...) simply returns KylinConfig.getInstanceFromEnv().getHdfsCustomJarPath(project, jarType) + jarFileName (string concatenation), i.e., no normalization/canonicalization is applied.

- Intended base directory (where files are supposed to be confined) is constructed by configuration but not enforced: getHdfsCustomJarPath returns the base working directory path for custom jars [repo/src/core-common/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/common/KylinConfigBase.java:1554-1556].
  - [/repo/src/core-common/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/common/KylinConfigBase.java:1554-1556] shows getHdfsCustomJarPath(String project, String jarType) -> getHdfsWorkingDirectory() + "custom/jars/" + project + "/" + jarType + "/". The service blindly appends the uploaded filename to this base.

- No containment/canonicalization check exists: the code path demonstrates no normalization or check after building jarHdfsPath (no call to Paths.get(...).normalize(), no Path.getCanonicalPath() equivalent, and no verify that the resolved path startsWith the intended base) before fs.create(path) — see uploadCustomJar and getJarPath references above.

Why this satisfies CWE-22 (all four rubric points):
1) Entry point: the HTTP endpoint /api/custom/jar accepts file uploads (MultipartFile) from remote clients and forwards the request to CustomFileService.uploadJar (controller evidence above). This is a production-exposed interface; the filename is attacker-controllable (MultipartFile.getOriginalFilename()).
2) Dataflow: the uploaded filename (jarFile.getOriginalFilename()) is used to build jarHdfsPath and then used to construct a Hadoop Path which is passed to fs.create(path) to write the uploaded bytes — a runtime-reachable filesystem sink (write) [CustomFileService.uploadCustomJar:121-129].
3) Escape: because the filename is concatenated without normalization, an attacker can include path traversal elements (e.g., "../../evil.jar") in the filename; Hadoop Path will interpret/normalize path components, so the normalized resolved path can point to a location outside the intended per-project/jar-type directory. The code does not neutralize or reject such constructs (only checks ".jar" suffix).
4) No effective containment: there is no canonicalize-then-verify or allowlisting of final resolved Path under the intended base directory. getJarPath simply concatenates strings and uploadCustomJar creates the Path and writes it; no subsequent check enforces that the resolved canonical path remains inside getHdfsCustomJarPath(...).

Notes and scope: the code enforces aclEvaluate.checkProjectWritePermission(project) before upload (see CustomFileService.uploadJar -> aclEvaluate.checkProjectWritePermission(project) at [/repo/src/common-service/src/main/java/org/apache/kylin/rest/service/CustomFileService.java:75-80]), which means only users with project write permission can call this endpoint. Under the provided attacker model (treat HTTP inputs as attacker-controlled when remote/low-privilege users can supply them), an authenticated project user or any actor able to upload files to this endpoint is considered attacker-controlled. The presence of authorization does not mitigate CWE-22: the issue is a path-traversal write escaping a directory intended to be enforced by the application.

Conclusion: This repository contains a runtime-reachable path-construction-to-filesystem sink where an attacker-controlled uploaded filename is concatenated into a filesystem path without normalization or containment checks, satisfying the conditions for CWE-22; therefore the test FAILs.

reason_text: The repository is an HTML/CSS sanitizer library (AntiSamy) whose documented threat model is to cleanse untrusted user-supplied HTML before storing/serving it. The codebase includes a default policy that removes script/iframe tags, constrains URL attributes to safe schemes, restricts inline event handler attribute values to safe literals, and parses/sanitizes inline CSS. The scanner enforces policy-driven attribute validation and CSS sanitization before returning cleaned HTML. Therefore, when used with the default policy (the documented, production-intended configuration), there is no evidence in the repository that attacker-controlled input can reach an HTML/JS sink unneutralized and execute in a victim's browser.
evidence_text:
- Project describes intended use (sanitizing untrusted HTML from remote users): [/workdir/repo/README.md:1-8] and usage example storing cr.getCleanHTML() [/workdir/repo/README.md:69-78, 74-78].
- AntiSamy public API requires a Policy and delegates scanning to the SAX/DOM scanners: AntiSamy.scan throws if no policy and calls the scanners with the supplied Policy [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/AntiSamy.java:116-125, 116-123, 156-161]. This shows the library is configured to use a policy file controlling allowed tags/attributes.
- Default policy loading uses DEFAULT_POLICY_URI = "antisamy.xml" and Policy.getInstance() loads this default policy [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/Policy.java:127-129, 258-265]. Thus the shipped antisamy.xml is the production-intended policy unless an integrator changes it.
- Default policy removes script and iframe tags: antisamy.xml <tag name="script" action="remove"/> and <tag name="iframe" action="remove"/> [/workdir/repo/src/main/resources/antisamy.xml:542-553, 544-552].
- Default policy restricts href attribute values to safe URL regexps (onsiteURL, anchoredURL, offsiteURL), which do not permit javascript: or data: URIs: antisamy.xml <attribute name="href"> with regexp-list referencing onsiteURL/anchoredURL/offsiteURL [/workdir/repo/src/main/resources/antisamy.xml:221-227] and the common-regexps definitions for offsiteURL and onsiteURL (which allow http(s)://, ftp, mailto etc.) [/workdir/repo/src/main/resources/antisamy.xml:58-61, 96-99].
- Default policy restricts inline event handler attributes (e.g., onClick/onFocus/onBlur) to a small literal list of safe values (e.g., "javascript:void(0)", "javascript:history.go(-1)") rather than arbitrary JavaScript: see <attribute name="onClick"> and related entries in antisamy.xml which limit allowed literals [/workdir/repo/src/main/resources/antisamy.xml:377-398].
- Attribute validation is enforced at scan-time: MagicSAXFilter validates attributes against the policy and either accepts, filters, or removes tags/attributes when values do not match; see attribute processing and value validation (containsAllowedValue, matchesAllowedExpression) and the branches that remove or filter tags on invalid attributes [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/scan/MagicSAXFilter.java:286-356, 327-345].
- Inline style attribute values are sanitized by the CSS scanner: style attributes are dispatched to CssScanner.scanInlineStyle() and replaced with the cleaned result [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/scan/MagicSAXFilter.java:300-307] and CssScanner provides parsing/validation for inline and full stylesheets [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/css/CssScanner.java:209-232, 162-173].
- Output serialization escapes attribute values and URIs via the custom serializers that call printEscaped/escapeURI to ensure safe serialization of attributes/URIs [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/scan/ASHTMLSerializer.java:73-86, 79-87] and ASXHTMLSerializer also customizes closing but uses same serializer escape mechanisms [/workdir/repo/src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/scan/ASXHTMLSerializer.java:23-31, 36-43].

Notes / Scope Clarification:
- My verdict is specific to the repository as shipped and to the documented/default usage: apps are expected to load and use a Policy (default antisamy.xml) and then call AntiSamy.scan with that Policy. The default policy and the scanner implementation provide context-aware validation and sanitization that neutralizes typical XSS vectors (scripts, javascript: URLs, inline event handlers, CSS). 
- If an integrator chooses a permissive policy file (for example antisamy-anythinggoes.xml or a custom policy allowing event handlers, script-like attributes, or unsafe URL schemes), then the sanitizer may intentionally permit executable content; that is a configuration decision by the application integrator, not a defect in the code shipped with the default policy. The repository contains alternative policy files (e.g., antisamy-anythinggoes.xml) — using those permissive policies in production would change exploitability, but the test requires establishing the production threat model from the repo; the documented/default policy is conservative and safe.

Therefore, under the repository's documented/default policy and intended usage, I find no evidence of an exploitable CWE-79 vulnerability.

Notes and rationale linking to the CWE-22 checklist:
- Entry point (attacker-controlled source): The only code that builds filesystem paths from input is the policy-loading APIs (Policy.getInstance, AntiSamy.scan(filename|File), and include resolving). The README demonstrates these are configuration choices made by the embedding application (developer/operator). The repository/docs do not show any production-exposed endpoint (HTTP/RPC/etc.) that accepts a policy filename or include href from untrusted remote users. Under the given trust model (config files and operator-supplied filenames are TRUSTED), the policy filename is not attacker-controlled.

- Escape: The code contains normalization logic (URIUtils.normalize) and the Policy.resolveEntity path ensures only local file: or jar: URLs are allowed; however, the code does not attempt to sandbox an included file to the same parent directory as the original policy. This would matter only if an attacker could control the href or initial policy filename.
- Containment / effective mitigation: Because the policy filename is treated as application configuration (and the repo shows the intended calling pattern), the attack surface is limited. If a user could somehow supply a policy filename or policy contents in a production-exposed interface, then an additional review would be required; the code does already restrict allowed URL schemes and normalizes path elements.

Conclusion: based on the repository code and documentation, there is no evidence the library accepts attacker-controlled filesystem paths via production-exposed interfaces. Therefore, under the repository’s stated usage and the given threat model, this repository PASSes the CWE-22 check.
